step4.objective:
• Each speed supported by the port configurable as an explicit fixed value, with the operational speed matching the configured value.
  • Auto-negotiation reported as disabled on a port carrying an explicit fixed speed, distinguishing a forced speed from a negotiated one in the port's reported state.
  • A link re-established at the newly configured speed after each speed change, without a device restart.
  • The port returned to its default negotiated behaviour when the fixed speed is removed or set back to auto.
  • A speed value that is invalid, out of range, or unsupported on the port's media type rejected with a clear error, the previous valid configuration remaining in effect.
  • No link established, and no spurious link-up reported, while the link partner is fixed at an incompatible speed — the link returning once the partner is set to a compatible value.
  • The configured fixed speed retained across an administrative shutdown/no-shutdown cycle and reapplied from saved configuration after a device restart.
  • Fixed speed applied per port, with configuration of one port leaving the speed and link state of other ports unchanged.
  • Configured speed and operational speed reported consistently in port status and configuration output.

provenance.objective_response:
• A fixed 1G copper port whose operational speed matches each explicitly configured fixed speed within the port's supported set (10, 100, 1000), with link established and traffic forwarding at that rate.
  • A duplex setting consistent with the configured fixed speed, with full-duplex operation available at every supported fixed-speed setting and half-duplex accepted only where the port type permits it.
  • Auto-negotiation disabled on the port when a fixed speed is configured, and the negotiation state reported accordingly on both the local port and the link partner.
  • A link that re-establishes at the newly configured speed following each speed change, without requiring a device reload.
  • The default port state restored when speed configuration is removed or set to auto, with auto-negotiation re-enabled and the link re-established at the highest mutually supported rate.
  • A rejected configuration attempt, with an explanatory error message and no change to the running configuration, when a speed outside the port's supported set (for example 2500, 5000, 10000, 40000) is requested on a fixed 1G copper port.
  • A rejected or non-applied configuration attempt for an invalid, malformed, or out-of-range speed value, with the previously configured speed retained and the link undisturbed.
  • A rejected speed/duplex combination that is not permitted by the port type, with the port remaining on its last valid setting.
  • A link that remains down, with no speed negotiation and no spurious link-up reporting, when the configured fixed speed is incompatible with the link partner's configured or supported speed.
  • A port that returns to a linked state at the correct speed once the partner is reconfigured to a compatible setting, without further local configuration.
  • An administratively shut down port that retains its configured fixed speed across the shutdown/no-shutdown cycle and relinks at that speed on re-enable.
  • Fixed-speed configuration preserved in the startup configuration and reapplied after a device reboot, with the port linking at the configured speed post-reboot.
  • Cable insertion and removal handled cleanly on a fixed-speed port, with link-down and link-up transitions reported and the configured speed reapplied on reinsertion.
  • Independent per-port speed settings, with configuration of one port leaving the speed, duplex, and link state of other ports unchanged.
  • Consistent speed configuration across ports configured as a group or range, with each member port reporting the same applied speed.
  • Configured speed, operational speed, duplex, auto-negotiation state, and link status consistently reported across interface status, interface detail, and running-configuration outputs.
  • The set of speeds advertised or listed as supported for the port reflecting only the capabilities of fixed 1G copper hardware.
  • Log entries and interface counters recording link state transitions and speed changes with accurate timestamps and port identification.
  • Management-interface views (for example status queries or network management protocol objects) reporting the same speed, duplex, and link state as the command-line outputs.
  • Error and rejection events surfaced to the operator through the applicable notification channels, with sufficient detail to identify the offending port and requested value.

steps.description: Note: Related ART Tests linked in Traceability.

With the DUT connected to a link partner over a link, and both ends at their default auto-negotiated settings, establish a baseline. Confirm the link comes up and record the negotiated speed, duplex and auto-negotiation state reported for the port.

Configure the port to each fixed speed the port supports in turn (checking both fibre and copper tranceivers where applicable), setting the link partner to a matching fixed speed for each. For every value, confirm the link re-establishes without restarting the device and that the operational speed matches the configured value.

With a fixed speed in effect on the port, inspect the port's reported state. Confirm auto-negotiation is reported as disabled, distinguishing the forced speed from the negotiated baseline recorded earlier.

Compare the configured speed against the operational speed for a port carrying a fixed speed, using both the port status view and the running configuration view. Confirm the two views agree with each other and with the value that was applied.

Remove the fixed speed from the port, and separately set it back to auto, with the link partner left auto-negotiating. Confirm the port returns to its default negotiated behaviour and that auto-negotiation is once again reported as enabled.

Attempt to configure speed values that are invalid, outside the supported range, and valid on other media but unsupported on this port. Confirm each attempt is rejected with a clear error and that the port's previously applied speed and link state are unaffected.

Fix the DUT port at one supported speed and fix the link partner at a different, incompatible speed. Confirm no link is established and that no spurious link-up is reported over a sustained observation period, then set the partner to a compatible speed and confirm the link returns.

With a fixed speed configured, administratively shut down the port and bring it back up. Confirm the fixed speed and auto-negotiation state are retained across the cycle and that the link re-establishes at the configured speed.

Save the configuration with a fixed speed applied and restart the device. Confirm the fixed speed is reapplied from saved configuration at startup and that the link comes up at that speed without further operator action.

With multiple ports linked to partners, apply a fixed speed to one port only. Confirm the configured speed, operational speed and link state of the other ports are unchanged, then repeat by changing the fixed speed on that port while the others remain linked.

The tester reads the objective and the step and reasons out what should happen; stating the outcome narrows them to producing exactly that result instead of evidence that the feature works. The objective already carries the expected outcomes. - Say WHAT is being exercised, not which command to type. Confirm neighbours are discovered on the test link and that each side reports the other's chassis and port identity.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Vary the transmit interval and hold multiplier across their supported range, including the minimum and maximum. Confirm advertisements are sent at the configured rate and that the neighbour's advertised lifetime tracks the configured values.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Set the transmit interval below the supported minimum and above the supported maximum. Confirm the DUT rejects both and retains its previous configuration.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Disable LLDP transmit on the DUT while leaving receive enabled, then re-enable it. Confirm the neighbour ages out and is rediscovered, and that the port reports the change.", "expectedResult": "" } ] Output the JSON array ONLY. No prose, no markdown fence.

• Each speed supported by the port configurable as an explicit fixed value, with the operational speed matching the configured value.
  • Auto-negotiation reported as disabled on a port carrying an explicit fixed speed, distinguishing a forced speed from a negotiated one in the port's reported state.
  • A link re-established at the newly configured speed after each speed change, without a device restart.
  • The port returned to its default negotiated behaviour when the fixed speed is removed or set back to auto.
  • A speed value that is invalid, out of range, or unsupported on the port's media type rejected with a clear error, the previous valid configuration remaining in effect.
  • No link established, and no spurious link-up reported, while the link partner is fixed at an incompatible speed — the link returning once the partner is set to a compatible value.
  • The configured fixed speed retained across an administrative shutdown/no-shutdown cycle and reapplied from saved configuration after a device restart.
  • Fixed speed applied per port, with configuration of one port leaving the speed and link state of other ports unchanged.
  • Configured speed and operational speed reported consistently in port status and configuration output.

gaps: The selected ART coverage exercises link establishment across supported speeds on fixed copper (1346.1001.20, 1346.1002.1) including specific fixed-speed points such as 10M and 40G, CLI-driven speed configuration and bundle interaction (1342.301.12), and console speed persistence across reboot (6009.2000.75853), so the core fixed-speed negotiation and configuration paths are reasonably addressed. Not well covered is the negative path central to this case: forcing an unsupported or mismatched fixed speed against a hub or legacy partner and observing that the port correctly remains down rather than reporting a misleading link state. Automation also does not address the 'ecofriendly lpi' configuration interaction with fixed-speed copper links, nor the associated power-saving/EEE behaviour when the peer does not support it. Observability aspects drawn from the manual case — port status column reporting, and the console-speed checks reflected in the Zephyr cross-references — remain largely manual, as does the QSFP-side speed configuration behaviour, which falls outside the fixed 1G copper scope of the automated set.
